messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Layla's Story

Layla was seventy-seven when she first came to the clinic on a Tuesday morning in October, moving carefully through the waiting room and choosing a chair positioned where she could see both the door and the hallway beyond. She had lived in the United States for forty-two years, but the weight of what she carried had not diminished with time or distance. In 1982, when she was thirty-five, the neighborhood where she lived in Beirut had been shelled during the civil war. She had been standing in her kitchen preparing lunch when the first explosion came—not a distant rumble but a percussion that seemed to detonate inside her own chest, followed by the shriek of shrapnel and the collapse of her neighbor's wall into the street. The building shook. Dust filled her lungs. For three hours she sheltered in a basement with strangers, listening to the percussion of impacts above, certain with each one that the next would bring the roof down. When she finally emerged, the street she had walked every day of her adult life was unrecognizable—rubble, blood, a child's shoe lying alone on the pavement. She had escaped with her life and eventually made her way to America, but the terror of that day had never truly left her.

For decades, Layla had managed. She had built a quiet life as a tutor, working with high school students in reading and writing from a small office in a strip mall. She had friends, routines, a modest apartment. But over the past eighteen months, something had shifted. The memories had grown sharper, more intrusive. When she closed her eyes at night, she was back in that basement—the smell of concrete and fear, the vibration of each distant impact traveling through her body as though it were happening now, in real time. The terror was not a memory of terror; it was terror itself, undiminished by decades. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to really think about what had happened, to sit with it fully, she would shatter. The thought itself was unbearable, so she had learned not to think about it. She avoided films, news programs, anything that might touch on conflict or violence. She did not speak about Lebanon. She did not allow herself to remember.

But avoidance had its own logic, one that tightened around her in ways she had not anticipated. At the tutoring center, she had begun to position herself differently in her small office—always near the door, always able to see the hallway. Her students had started to notice. One had asked if she was uncomfortable working with him; another's parent had inquired whether Layla was well. She had made excuses. What she could not articulate was that she felt weak for needing to do this, ashamed that at her age she could not simply sit in a room without calculating exits. The belief that she was fundamentally fragile, that she lacked the strength others possessed, had taken root. This conviction seemed to justify her avoidance—of course she needed to stay near the door; of course she could not watch the news; of course she could not dwell on the past. She was not strong enough to face these things. And yet, each time she avoided, each time she rearranged her office or changed the channel or turned away from a memory, the belief deepened. She felt dead inside most days, numb to the world around her, as though the part of her that had survived that day in Beirut was all that remained—a hollow shell going through the motions of living.

The memories themselves had become unpredictable tormentors. A car backfiring outside the tutoring center sent her heart into her throat, and suddenly she was in the basement again, bracing for impact. A student mentioning a trip to the Middle East triggered the full sensory recall—not just the memory of terror but the terror itself, flooding through her body without warning. Because she had trained herself not to think about the event, these intrusions felt all the more violent, arriving from nowhere like the explosions themselves. She had no way to prepare, no mental framework to contain them. The more she avoided thinking about it, the more the memories seemed to own her, breaking through her defenses at unpredictable moments and pulling her back into that basement, that street, that impossible afternoon. By October, when she finally called the clinic, Layla was exhausted—not from the memories themselves but from the endless work of running from them, from the conviction that she was too weak to face what had happened, and from the terrible irony that her attempts to protect herself had only made her more vulnerable to the very thing she feared most.
